Three clients (web UI, dpi-tui, curl) reach durable agents on four devices; the clients disconnect and every device keeps checkpointing its run to SQLite

Pi Durable, from the team behind the Pi coding agent, persists ongoing work, conversations and application state through failures, through clients and through change itself. This repo puts it to work. Every device runs a small server, `dpi-backend`, that owns its agents, their SQLite databases and their tools. Clients connect with a **URL and a bearer token**: a web hub that watches every device at once, `dpi-tui` in the terminal, or one `curl` that sends work and waits for the answer. **The agent lives on the device, not in the client.** Close the browser, quit the terminal or restart the machine mid-tool, and the run picks up from its last checkpoint.

The OpenID Foundation's October 2025 whitepaper on Identity Management for Agentic AI identifies this as the industry's most urgent unsolved problem: *"User impersonation by agents should be replaced by delegated authority. True delegation requires explicit 'on-behalf-of' flows where agents prove their delegated scope while remaining identifiable as distinct from the user they represent."*
|Real-time revocation with cascade|❌|❌|✅ CAE / SSF signals|

- **DPoP Sender-Constrained Tokens** — RFC 9449. Clients may attach a `DPoP` proof JWT to any `/oauth2/token` call; the issued token then carries `cnf.jkt` and `token_type: "DPoP"`. Proof replay is blocked by an atomic `dpop_jti` upsert (DB primary key — no pre-check race). Resource servers retrieve `cnf` via introspection and validate the per-request proof themselves. Full reference: `docs/dpop-and-dcr.md`.

- **Dynamic Client Registration** — RFC 7591 (`POST /oauth2/register`) gated by an initial access token with the `client:register` scope, plus RFC 7592 management (`GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE /oauth2/register/{client_id}`) authenticated by a one-shot `registration_access_token` (bcrypt-hashed at rest, constant-time lookup). Internal admin-registered clients remain isolated from DCR — the delete path refuses to touch `registration_source = 'internal'`. Full reference: `docs/dpop-and-dcr.md`.

- **Scope ceilings** — an identity's `allowed_scopes` is the absolute ceiling of the scopes its tokens can carry (the RFC 7591 client `scope` equivalent); credential policies are reusable bundles that only narrow within it. Every grant intersects the request with every layer that restricts, token exchange narrows at each hop, and a grant whose layers leave nothing is refused rather than minted without scopes. Full reference: `docs/scope-ceilings.md`.

- **Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD)** — `draft-ietf-oauth-client-id-metadata-document`, the MCP Authorization 2026-07-28 preferred default. An agent onboards with **zero pre-registration** by using a stable `https://` URL as its `client_id`; on the `authorization_code` + PKCE flow ZeroID fetches the JSON metadata document that URL publishes, validates it (self-reference match, `redirect_uris` allow-list, `token_endpoint_auth_method` of `none` or `private_key_jwt`), and treats it as an ephemeral client — public PKCE, or key-authenticated against the key set the document publishes — nothing is persisted. The fetch reuses the same DNS-rebinding-safe SSRF-guarded HTTP client as attestation/CIBA (private/loopback/metadata ranges blocked, 5 KiB size cap, timeout), with an optional `allowed_domains` allowlist. Advertised as `client_id_metadata_document_supported` in AS metadata. On by default. Full reference: `docs/cimd.md`.

- **Rich Authorization Requests (RAR)** — RFC 9396. Agents can attach a typed `authorization_details` JSON array to a CIBA `/oauth2/bc-authorize` call describing exactly what is being authorized at finer granularity than `scope` — e.g. `{"type": "tool_call", "tool": "transfer_funds", "amount": 50000}`. The `BackchannelNotifier` receives the parsed typed slice so the approver UX can render a per-action prompt instead of "approve this scope." Per-type schema validation is opt-in via `Server.RegisterAuthorizationDetailValidator(typ, fn)`. JSON and form-encoded bodies both supported. Rejections map to the RFC 9396 `invalid_authorization_details` OAuth error code. Full reference: `docs/rar.md`.

- **On-Behalf-Of (OBO) Delegation** — RFC 8693 token exchange with automatic scope attenuation at each hop, delegation depth tracking, and cascade revocation when any upstream credential is revoked. Under the `rfc8693` token profile, `sub` stays the person or workload the chain acts for at every hop and the nested `act` claim carries every agent in it, current one outermost, closing the auditability gap that plagues shared service accounts. See Token profiles.

- **Attestation Framework** — Pluggable verifiers behind a fail-closed contract: software, platform, and hardware attestation elevate trust levels before credentials are issued. Ships with an OIDC verifier (GitHub Actions, GCP Workload Identity, Kubernetes projected SA tokens, etc.) plus per-tenant `AttestationPolicy` for issuer allowlisting and claim binding. Full reference: `docs/attestation.md`.

- **Trusted issuers** — agents registered in a customer IdP reach ZeroID with the IdP's own tokens: an ID-JAG redeemed with `jwt-bearer`, or the person's OpenID Connect ID token exchanged by the agent it was issued to (RFC 8693, `private_key_jwt` only, positively an ID token). Issuers are per-account rows (`federation.issuer_store: db`) of kind `person` or `workload`, read live on every grant, with credential bindings that map the agent to its own identity, the tenant derived rather than requested, adopted agents only, and a hook (`Server.SetFederatedPersonResolver`) that maps the IdP person to the deployer's user. Standalone deployments keep the static `external_issuers` list. Full reference: `docs/external-issuers.md`; a mock IdP for local runs is `cmd/zeroid-mockidp`.

**Refresh token rotation:** every `refresh_token` grant rotates — the presented refresh token is consumed and a new one is returned, in the same token family. A refresh token can be used once. Presenting one that has already been rotated is treated as a sign that the family has leaked (RFC 9700 §4.14.2): ZeroID revokes every refresh token in the family, including the newest, along with the access tokens issued from the family (and their delegated descendants), and answers `invalid_grant`, the same response as any other unusable refresh token. The exception is a short grace window after each rotation, `token.refresh_reuse_grace_seconds` (env `ZEROID_REFRESH_REUSE_GRACE_SECONDS`, default 10, range 0–300): within it, a second presentation of the rotated-out token is refused with `invalid_grant` as a concurrent retry and nothing is revoked, so tabs or processes that share one refresh token and refresh at the same moment keep their session. The grace covers only rotation — a token whose family was revoked (reuse detection, RFC 7009 revocation, authorization-code replay) is refused outright — and its cost is that a stolen rotated-out token used within the window does not revoke the family. Set it to 0 for strict RFC 9700 behaviour, in which two concurrent refreshes with one token leave the family revoked. Clients should still serialise refreshes and keep only the newest refresh token. If the server fails after consuming the token but before answering, it puts the presented token back, so retrying with it rotates normally. To end a session, revoke the refresh token at `/oauth2/token/revoke` (RFC 7009): that revokes the family and its access tokens.

**A self-hosted PaaS that deploys any GitHub repo in under 3 minutes.**
#### Explained in more detail in docs
|**API Server**|Node.js, Express 5, TypeScript|Familiar, fast to iterate, typed end to end with Zod validation|
|**Queue**|BullMQ + Redis|Persistent jobs, retry logic, concurrency limiting|
|**Database**|PostgreSQL 16 + Prisma|State machine triggers enforced at DB layer, JSONB for metadata, tsvector for log search|
|**Build Runner**|build-engine container (`docker run` per build)|Isolated per-build environment, no shared state — the worker shells out through the host Docker socket|
|**Dynamic App Runtime**|Sibling Docker containers on a private compose network|Persistent containers, health-checked staged swaps on redeploy, no orchestration daemon needed|
|**Static Hosting**|MinIO (S3-compatible) + reverse-proxy streaming|Self-hosted object storage for build output, no running container at rest|
|**Edge Routing**|nginx (wildcard `*.domain`) + certbot TLS|Host-based routing to deployed apps, HTTPS via Let's Encrypt|
|**Container Images**|Locally built images (`docker build`, tagged per project)|No external registry — build-engine tags `dreamer-app:<slug>` and runs it directly|
|**Cache / PubSub**|Redis ×2 (ioredis) — platform + build events|Log streaming, container state, rate limiting; a second instance isolates noisy build pub/sub|
|**Frontend**|Next.js, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4|Server components for data-heavy pages, Socket.IO client for live updates|
|**Realtime**|Socket.IO (WebSocket)|Live build logs and deployment-state changes pushed from API server to dashboard|
|**Auth**|JWT (15min access) + httpOnly refresh cookie|XSS-resistant, token rotation, session revocation|
|**Secrets**|AES-256-GCM per-value encryption|Secrets never stored in plaintext, IV per value|
- Static apps → uploaded to MinIO, streamed by the reverse proxy. No running container at rest.
- Dynamic apps → a long-lived Docker container on the private compose network, routed by hostname through nginx → reverse-proxy.
|`QUEUED`|Build job created, waiting for a worker|`LAUNCHING`, `CANCELLED`, `FAILED`|
